I've recently learned that dish soap (or all soap for that matter) doesn't even kill bacteria, it simply helps in washing it away. For the past month or two I've been using dish soap less and less. When the food on a plate is still fresh I just run it under hot water and scrub it off with steel wool and as far as I can tell it's as clean as can be. Now with things that are really greasy like bacon fat, dish soap does help it come off easier but even still hot water and steel wool seems to be doing the trick just fine.

Is soap necessary? Or are we just buying something that is sort of redundant? ..thoughts, comments, concerns?
If you don't wash all of it off of the plates you end up eating it.

This also brings me to another point.. I believe as a society we've grown an unreasonable fear of bacteria, germs and expiring food. I used to always toss food once it hit the expiration date no matter what.. but based off some things I've heard and been told I've recently started to use my senses to judge a food's well-being rather than the number printed on the package. Our noses are incredibly useful mechanisms and will tell you instinctively when something has spoiled, coupled without eyes we have a great ability to sense if food is bad or not.

If there's mold growing on cheese then you just cut that section off.. most mold is actually benign and that's not even to mention cheese itself is a mold. I know people who'll eat food well beyond the expiration date and they're perfectly fine.. hell if anything I think it can be a boost to the immune system. Fearing away from germs and bacteria may be weakening our body's immune system to the point where any contact with a harmful bacteria will get us sick just because our bodies haven't been prepped to fight it off.

I recommend the site StillTasty

It has information on the shelf/fridge/freezer life and preservation methods.

When non alcohol soaps claim that they remove 99.999% of bacteria, they mean that bacteria is removed mechanically (with water and detergent soap suds) as opposed to bacteria being killed chemically (alcohol).

Soap IS better than no soap. I would still use somesoap. You don't have to duplicate dish soap in the sink and additional soap in a dishwasher though.

You should probably be good, especially if you are cleaning your plates right away. The hot water is probably not going to help if you don't use soap though. The water would have to be so hot to kill bacteria (143 F according to Louis Pasteur) that someone would get burned before the bacteria would be effectively killed.

Source: when I first graduated from college, I worked for a company that did 3rd-party testing, including a lot of dishwashers.

I'm not using hot water to kill bacteria (since soap itself doesn't do this) I'm just using the energy from pressurized steamy water to loosen up any food particle to wash them all down the drain. I'd be interested to see electron-microscope images of plates cleaned with soap vs hot water alone, I think it'd be an interesting study.

Soap is not used to kill bacteria, it for more easily removal fats. Fat remains on dishes can make then smell rancid. Most bacteria will die on clean plates in a relatively short time due to lack of "food".

Yes this has the main times I've been using soap, say if a pan was left overnight with beef/bacon fat in it I'll use some soap and steaming water to scrub it all out, but when that fat is still freshly cooked steaming water will clean it right off. If the pan's still really hot too then water will boil when I put it in which I've found works really well for cleaning as well.
Soap is not necessary, but it makes it a lot easier in the average case. If you get it clean some other way, that's no problem.

Consider the chemical structure of soap. One end is hydrophobic (does not like water) and one end is hydrophilic (likes water). The hydrophobic end grabs onto everything beside water and the hydrophilic end grabs onto water molecules and that is how soap removes dirt, food particles, etc. So use soap if you want to be cleaner at the molecular level.
